newsitem.title: GERMANY: MAN truck unit expects more favourable H2.
newsitem.headline: MAN truck unit expects more favourable H2.

text.p: The truck unit of Germany's group MAN AG said on Thursday it expected the second half of its fiscal year to develop more favourably than the first half, giving "positive" full-year results.

MAN Nutzfahrzeuge AG chief executive Rudolf Rupprecht told a news conference at the IAA truck exhibition that the group saw "a difficult general situation" in the German commercial vehicle market and overall tough competition in western Europe.

"We are assuming that the second half of our current fiscal year, which starts in 1997, will develop more favourably than has been the case with the first," Rupprecht said in the text of a speech for a company news conference at the exhibition.

"Providing this happens, we believe that with our up-to-date and technically sophisticated range of trucks and buses we will be able to complete the current fiscal year too with a positive result," he said.
The truck maker accounts for about 40 percent of MAN AG's annual revenues. MAN AG's fiscal year ends on June 30.
The MAN unit reported sales for the 1995/96 business year rose 10 percent to about eight billion marks($5.3 billion) and pre-tax profits rose 24 percent to about 50 million marks, he said.
"This is a result with which we can in principle be satisfied," he said, noting the tough industry conditions.
"However, this cannot disguise the fact that the general economic development and thus our current use of capacity demands greater efforts from us."
He said Germany's position in the European commercial vehicle market had been "problematic" and that the German market was "considerably more negative" than other areas.

In the category of trucks weighing 16 tonnes or more, Rupprecht said MAN had stabilised its German market share at 28 percent, while its share in the class from six to 11 tonnes had settled at about 20 percent in the domestic market.

Rupprecht noted that Germany and Austria, MAN's main markets, developed less strongly than those in the rest of Europe. But he said France, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain were still recording double-digit growth rates.
Overall in western Europe, Rupprecht said MAN improved its market share to eight percent and was also seeking to penetrate markets in eastern Europe and Turkey.
"For us, Turkey is as before of particular importance as a springboard for opening up the states in the south of the former Soviet Union and the markets of the Middle East," he said.
